value_text: Matures at ~2 years, most breed at 3-4 years, live up to 6 years, and females produce ~200-1200 eggs of 2.2-2.5 mm diameter.

location: Lake Pedder impoundment and some tributaries
value_text: Following inundation, Pedder galaxias was present in large numbers in the impoundment during 1975-1980 and in some tributaries.
model_use: supports short-lived post-flood boom phase
notes: Taxonomic confidence not absolute because early records precede improved museum screening of Pedder v. climbing galaxias.

value_text: Wild brown trout in the upper Huon were supplemented with a one-off stocking of 350,000 brown trout fry in September 1972.
model_use: external forcing for trout pressure trajectory
notes: Corroborative official source; primary stocking records remain a priority retrieval target.

value_text: After the 1972 stocking, brown trout quickly averaged 4.5-8 kg before a later bust to average sizes of ~0.4-0.8 kg, with some to 1.2 kg.
model_use: qualitative indicator of an early prey-fuelled trout boom
notes: Useful as a rough corroborative signal, not as a precise quantitative series.

value_text: Anglers noted trout eating galaxiids throughout the mid-late 1970s and very early 1980s.
model_use: supports early trout predation pressure
notes: Important chronology signal but not quantified.

value_text: In the 1988 survey, only one Pedder galaxias specimen was collected and climbing galaxias was the most commonly found species.
model_use: strong late-decline constraint for tributary occupancy

value_text: The 1989 survey found only a few Pedder galaxias in two small streams, whereas climbing galaxias was again widely distributed.
model_use: chronology of narrowing refugia and climbing expansion

value_text: Between 1988 and 1991, 117 sites were surveyed and Pedder galaxias was found at only 5 of them.
model_use: late-interval occupancy benchmark

value_text: Only 68 Pedder galaxias were captured in 43 trips to the two Bonnet Bay creeks from February 1990 to September 1991.
model_use: relative abundance benchmark for final refugia

value_text: Museum screening indicated Pedder galaxias dominated lake samples up to about 1980, whereas climbing galaxias became more abundant from about 1983 onwards.
model_use: constraint on lagged climbing expansion
notes: Based on few samples but taxonomic screening used vertebral counts.

value_text: Limited samples suggest Pedder galaxias was already declining in the lake before climbing galaxias became abundant, implying climbing galaxias probably hastened rather than initiated decline.
model_use: supports joint-cause hypothesis with trout-first sequence

habitat: littoral food web and water quality
value_text: Collapse in food supply or water quality alone was considered unlikely to explain Pedder galaxias decline.
model_use: reason to treat habitat-only model as a null foil rather than a favored explanation

value_text: The most likely factors causing Pedder galaxias decline were predation and competition with both brown trout and climbing galaxias.
model_use: core competing-mechanisms set

value_text: Sanger concluded Lake Pedder was and would likely remain a hostile environment for reintroduction because trout and climbing galaxias remained widespread in the lake and tributaries.
model_use: frames management counterfactuals and endpoint plausibility

location: Lake Pedder, Wedge River, Lake Gordon, McPartlans canal
value_text: After flooding, the distribution of Pedder galaxias initially increased throughout the new lake and into the adjacent Wedge River, Lake Gordon and McPartlans canal.
model_use: supports an early expansion/boom phase before collapse

value_text: Late-1980s surveys restricted Pedder galaxias to four tributary streams, early-1990s surveys to two tributary streams, and 1994-1997 surveys collected only five specimens.
model_use: multi-step chronology of final natural-range collapse

value_text: Extensive IFS surveys between 1998 and 2002 did not locate the species anywhere in its natural range.
model_use: extirpation endpoint constraint

value_text: The Lake Oberon translocated population was surveyed in January 2001 and estimated to include ~500 adults plus many pelagic juveniles.
model_use: baseline intrinsic growth in predator-free refuge

value_text: The EPBC assessment states that 52 adults were moved from Lake Oberon to Strathgordon, with a further 22 fish added in March 2002.
model_use: starting conditions for Strathgordon population
notes: Equivalent to the 74 adults later summarized in the 2006 recovery plan.

value_text: A total of 34 fish were transferred to Lake Oberon between 1991 and 1997 and the population became established.
model_use: refuge-population founding size
notes: Conflicts with Sanger 2001 reporting 42 fish released in 1991-1992.

value_text: Sanger reported that 42 Pedder galaxias were released to Lake Oberon between November 1991 and November 1992.
model_use: records a source discrepancy that should be resolved before formal demographic modeling
notes: Keep unresolved until Hamr 1992, Gaffney et al. 1992, and detailed translocation logs are obtained.

value_text: The 2006 recovery plan reports 74 adults moved to Strathgordon in 2001 and 2002, with no successful breeding confirmed as of June 2004.
model_use: early performance benchmark for artificial refuge population

value_text: Captive breeding in 1990-91 produced only 11 juveniles.
model_use: illustrates limited captive-breeding feasibility and low fallback options

value_text: By the 2006 recovery plan, the Lake Oberon population was estimated to include a minimum of 500 adults and was described as thriving.
model_use: upper-end refuge demography in fish-free habitat

value_text: Chilcott et al. concluded the conservation program, specifically translocation, saved Pedder galaxias from extinction and that the species was then known from only two translocated populations.
model_use: confirms long-run recovery narrative and management significance of translocations
notes: Full paper should still be obtained for detailed methods and monitoring history.

location: Lake Oberon and Strathgordon water supply dam
value_text: Current official status is that no extant populations remain in original habitat, while Lake Oberon and Strathgordon populations are both abundant and self-sustaining.
model_use: current endpoint for ex situ baseline dynamics

value_text: The listing statement notes Strathgordon is now self-sustaining through natural recruitment.
model_use: supports use of Strathgordon as a Pedder baseline site despite earlier failed breeding
notes: Source explicitly cites Chilcott et al. 2013.

value_text: In April 2023, 214 Pedder galaxias were captured from 12 fyke nets at Strathgordon, giving a CPUE of 17.8 fish per net; young-of-the-year recruitment was absent in the length data.
model_use: modern translocated-population abundance and recruitment benchmark

value_text: In April 2025, 89 Pedder galaxias were captured from 16 fyke nets at Strathgordon, giving 5.6 fish per net; the report attributes the lower abundance to limited recruitment in 2022-2024.
model_use: current sign of recruitment variability in ex situ population

location: Lake Pedder, western shore and Hermit Basin
value_text: A focused 2016 electrofishing survey in Lake Pedder found numerous brown trout (130-400 mm) and climbing galaxias, confirming key threat taxa remain present; no redfin perch were detected.
model_use: confirms present-day unsuitability of Lake Pedder reintroduction without threat control
